source.section: The values and principles of the UK
source.reviewer_note: Check page; list of fundamental principles

question_text: Which TWO of these are fundamental principles of British life?

options.rationale: Voting is a right, not a legal duty, in the UK.

options.text: Tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs

explanation_simple: The principles include democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance of different faiths and beliefs, and taking part in community life.

question_text: Which countries make up the United Kingdom?

options.text: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland

options.rationale: These three make up Great Britain, not the whole UK.

options.text: England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland
England, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man

explanation_simple: The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Great Britain means England, Scotland and Wales only.
memory_tip: Great Britain is the big island; the UK adds Northern Ireland.

question_text: Is the following statement TRUE or FALSE? The Isle of Man is part of the United Kingdom.
explanation_simple: The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands are Crown dependencies. They are linked to the UK but are not part of it, and have their own governments.

question_text: In which year did William, Duke of Normandy, defeat King Harold at the Battle of Hastings?

options.rationale: 1215 is the year of the Magna Carta.

explanation_simple: William of Normandy invaded England and defeated Harold at Hastings in 1066. This began the Norman Conquest.
memory_tip: Ten-sixty-six: the last successful invasion of England.

question_text: In 1215 King John was forced by his noblemen to agree to a charter that limited the king's power. What is it called?

options.rationale: The Bill of Rights dates from 1689.
The Domesday Book was a survey ordered by William the Conqueror.

explanation_simple: The Magna Carta (the Great Charter) of 1215 established that even the king was subject to the law.

question_text: Which TWO of these women were wives of King Henry VIII?
explanation_simple: Henry VIII married six times: Catherine of Aragon, Anne Boleyn, Jane Seymour, Anne of Cleves, Catherine Howard and Catherine Parr.
memory_tip: Divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived.

question_text: The Act of Union of 1707 created the Kingdom of Great Britain. Which two countries did it join?

options.rationale: Ireland was united with Great Britain in 1801.

explanation_simple: In 1707 England (already united with Wales) and Scotland became one country, the Kingdom of Great Britain. Scotland kept its own legal and education systems.

question_text: In which year was the Battle of Britain fought in the skies over Britain?
explanation_simple: In the summer of 1940 the Royal Air Force fought the German air force over Britain. Britain's victory meant Germany could not invade.

question_text: Who is the patron saint of Wales, whose day is celebrated on 1 March?

options.rationale: St Andrew is the patron saint of Scotland (30 November).
St George is the patron saint of England (23 April).
St Patrick is the patron saint of Northern Ireland (17 March).

explanation_simple: St David's Day is 1 March. The other patron saints' days are St Patrick (17 March), St George (23 April) and St Andrew (30 November).
memory_tip: In calendar order: David, Patrick, George, Andrew.

source.section: The UK government, the law and your role
source.reviewer_note: Handbook states 18 for UK Parliament elections; do not mention later Scottish/Welsh changes unless handbook does

question_text: According to the handbook, what is the minimum age for voting in UK Parliament elections?
explanation_simple: The handbook gives 18 as the voting age for UK Parliament elections.

question_text: Which of these statements is correct?

options.text: Parliament is made up of the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
Parliament is made up of the House of Commons and the Senate.

explanation_simple: The UK Parliament has two houses: the elected House of Commons and the House of Lords, whose members are not elected.

question_text: How often must a general election be held in the UK?
explanation_simple: MPs are elected at a general election, which is held at least every five years.
